Contaminated Oral Liquid Medicines, India

WHO Medical Product Alert N°5/2025 names specific batches of three oral liquid medicines found to contain diethylene glycol (DEG), reported to WHO by India’s CDSCO on 8 October 2025 after clusters of acute illness and child deaths.

Evidence assistant

EVIDENCE ASSISTANTSCRIPTED · NO AI MODEL RUNS HERE

Answers are assembled by fixed rules from this record and the official alerts on this site. Every answer links to its evidence and says so when a connection cannot be established. It cannot diagnose, establish causality or confirm a hypothesis.

SUGGESTED QUESTIONS

Verified facts

Stated in an official document read directly, or reported by two or more independent outlets.

  • On 30 September 2025, WHO identified information on localised clusters of acute illness and child fatalities in India.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • On 8 October 2025, CDSCO reported to WHO the presence of diethylene glycol in at least three oral liquid medicines.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[1][2]

  • CDSCO informed WHO that the contaminated products were reportedly consumed by the affected children.

    “reportedly consumed by the affected children”
    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • The contaminated medicines are specific batches of COLDRIF, Respifresh TR and ReLife.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • State authorities ordered an immediate halt to production at the implicated sites, suspended product authorisations and initiated a recall.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[1][2]

  • CDSCO informed WHO that none of the contaminated medicines had been exported and there was no evidence of illegal export.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • WHO advised regulators to evaluate oral liquid medicines from the same manufacturing sites, particularly those produced since December 2024.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

Reported claims

Reported by one outlet and not independently confirmed.

Nothing in this record falls here.

Unknown or not established

The sources say this is unknown or was not shown.

Nothing in this record falls here.

Reported health concerns

  • Diethylene glycol is toxic to humans when consumed and can prove fatal. Use, especially in children, may result in serious injury or death.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • Toxic effects listed by WHO include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, inability to pass urine, headache, altered mental state and acute kidney injury, which may lead to death.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • The alert describes clusters of acute illness and child fatalities, but gives no number of cases or deaths.

    NOT ESTABLISHED[2]

Regulatory actions

  • State authorities ordered an immediate halt to production at the implicated manufacturing sites.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • State authorities suspended product authorisations and initiated a recall of the contaminated products.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • WHO advised regulators to consider targeted market surveillance, especially of informal and unregulated supply chains.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

  • WHO asked authorities to notify it immediately if these products are detected in their country.

    OFFICIAL SOURCE[2]

Evidence gaps

  • The alert does not state where the illnesses occurred or how many children were affected.
  • The source of the contamination was still being identified when the alert was published.
  • Only the listed batches are named; the alert does not say whether other batches were tested.
